# The RSI Tax: When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost

Yitong Zhang Affiliation: School of Physics, Peking University    Ang Li
Affiliation: State Key Lab of General Artificial Intelligence,School of
Intelligence Science and Technology, Peking University    Yisen Wang
Affiliation: State Key Lab of General Artificial Intelligence,School of
Intelligence Science and Technology, Peking University

###### Abstract

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) seeks to improve an agent using its own
task experience. Its practical value depends on whether performance
gains justify the full cost of self-improvement and task execution. We
evaluate this trade-off on continual task streams, scoring each task
before its feedback is used for subsequent updates. We define the _RSI
Tax_ as the token cost of the self-improvement process and include it
alongside task-execution costs in end-to-end evaluation. Across six
methods and two language models, a bounded-note baseline matches or
exceeds the observed accuracy of Meta-Harness, EvoSkill, and RRSI, with
mean total-token savings of 65.6–71.0%. We decompose the RSI Tax into
verification, exploration, and writing costs, and track subsequent use
of the associated state or artifact. For these three RSI methods,
verification accounts for 74.8–93.6% of the aggregate RSI Tax. A
substantial share of the RSI Tax is also associated with states or
artifacts that are not used later in the evaluated streams. These
results expose a practical limitation of costly RSI procedures:
improvements in the deployed agent need not justify the expense of the
improvement process. They motivate RSI objectives that jointly optimize
the RSI Tax and expected task-execution cost while ensuring continued
growth in agent capabilities across the task stream.

## 1 Introduction

Large language model (LLM) agents use tools to perform software
development and other professional tasks \[[1](#bib.bib1),
[2](#bib.bib2), [3](#bib.bib3), [4](#bib.bib4)\]. During continued use,
an agent may encounter related tasks within the same repository or
application. Retaining useful procedures and lessons from failures could
reduce repeated exploration and improve later task performance. Recent
sequential benchmarks examine this reuse through connected workflows,
related task variants, and skill accumulation \[[5](#bib.bib5),
[6](#bib.bib6), [7](#bib.bib7)\].

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) uses task experience to update the
state an agent carries into subsequent tasks. We focus on RSI with fixed
model weights and distinguish methods by the components they update. One
category of RSI maintains an evolving set of memories or skills for use
in later tasks \[[8](#bib.bib8), [9](#bib.bib9), [10](#bib.bib10)\].
Another category modifies the agent’s harness, including the
instructions, tool interfaces, and control code used for task
execution \[[11](#bib.bib11), [12](#bib.bib12), [13](#bib.bib13)\].

The self-improvement process has a cost of its own. Recent studies
compare online auxiliary modules and task-level search under resource
constraints, and relate capability gains to learning
cost \[[14](#bib.bib14), [15](#bib.bib15), [16](#bib.bib16)\].
Validation-task selection and the amortization of skill-search cost are
also studied \[[17](#bib.bib17), [18](#bib.bib18)\]. On a task stream,
each update incurs a cost before its value for later tasks is known.
Task execution itself also varies in token demand across tasks, runs,
and models \[[19](#bib.bib19)\].

We call the token cost of the self-improvement process the _RSI Tax_. We
count the tokens spent attempting an update even when the agent
ultimately retains its previous state. End-to-end cost is the sum of
these update tokens and the tokens used to execute the task stream. The
two terms are coupled: an update can shorten later executions, but can
also add context or induce longer trajectories. The relevant trade-off
is between the agent’s capability gains over the task stream and this
combined token cost.

We compare six methods on repository and terminal task streams using two
backbone models. Our simple baseline, Simple Reflection with Notes
(SRN), revises one bounded note from completed failures without
candidate search. Across the four model–environment settings, SRN
matches or exceeds the observed accuracy of Meta-Harness, EvoSkill, and
RRSI while using 65.6–71.0% fewer total tokens on average, depending on
the comparison method
(Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost")).

To explain these differences, we decompose the RSI Tax into
_verification_, _exploration_, and _writing_. For these three RSI
methods, verification accounts for 74.8–93.6% of the RSI Tax after
aggregation over the four settings. We also track whether the associated
state or artifact is used by later tasks. Among the evaluated RSI
methods other than SRN, 23.7–63.6% of the RSI Tax is associated with
states or artifacts that are not used later in the observed stream.

Our results expose a gap between recursively improving an agent and
making the improvement process cost-effective. Our decomposition shows
that repeated verification can consume more tokens than task execution
itself, while substantial update costs are associated with artifacts
that are not used later. HarnessPro and RRSI already account for
execution cost in harness selection \[[13](#bib.bib13),
[12](#bib.bib12)\]. Their selection objectives do not, however, jointly
optimize the cost of obtaining updates and the expected cost of serving
a continuing task stream. Our findings therefore motivate policies that
choose when to update, how much to spend on proposals and validation,
and which artifacts to retain according to their expected contribution
to future task performance and token use. The goal is to sustain growth
in agent capabilities as tasks arrive while jointly optimizing the RSI
Tax and expected task-execution cost.

Figure 1: Streaming evaluation and the RSI Tax. (a) Updates use
completed-task feedback; SRN maintains a bounded note. (b) The RSI Tax
is broken down into verification, exploration, and writing costs. (c)
Accuracy averaged equally over the four settings. (d) Input-plus-output
tokens summed over those settings, including task execution, the three
RSI Tax components, and the Other residual. These sums describe token
volume across the runs; within-setting comparisons are reported in
Section [5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 Accuracy and End-to-End Cost ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost").

To summarize, our contributions are:

1.  1.  A streaming cost–performance evaluation. We compare six methods on
        common task streams and assess accuracy against end-to-end token
        cost, including the RSI Tax.
2.  2.  A simple adaptive baseline. SRN provides a counterexample to the
        need for costly update procedures to attain the performance observed
        in these experiments.
3.  3.  A decomposition of the RSI Tax. We separate verification,
        exploration, and writing costs, and link them to subsequent use of
        the associated state or artifact.

## 2 Evaluation Setup

### 2.1 RSI Methods and Evaluation Protocols

We study RSI that updates an agent’s persistent state while keeping its
backbone model fixed. One category of RSI updates the memories or skills
available to the agent during task execution. ReasoningBank extracts
strategies from completed trajectories and retrieves them for later
tasks \[[8](#bib.bib8)\]; Dynamic Cheatsheet maintains an evolving
note \[[9](#bib.bib9)\]. EvoSkill searches over reusable skill
folders \[[10](#bib.bib10)\], while SkillOpt applies bounded edits to
skill documents \[[20](#bib.bib20)\].

Another category modifies the harness that controls prompting, tool use,
and task execution. GEPA optimizes instructions using execution
feedback \[[21](#bib.bib21)\], and Meta-Harness searches over controller
code \[[11](#bib.bib11)\]. RRSI regularizes harness changes to
discourage benchmark-specific edits \[[12](#bib.bib12)\]; HarnessPro
considers execution cost as well as performance when selecting a
harness \[[13](#bib.bib13)\].

Evaluation procedures differ in when feedback becomes available and
where performance is measured. ReasoningBank updates memory between
successive tasks, whereas EvoSkill and RRSI optimize skills or harnesses
on a fixed task collection before evaluating the selected state on
held-out tasks or other benchmarks \[[8](#bib.bib8), [10](#bib.bib10),
[12](#bib.bib12)\]. EvoTest evaluates adaptation across repeated
episodes of the same game \[[22](#bib.bib22)\], whereas TTHE adapts to
an unlabeled current batch before scoring performance on that
batch \[[23](#bib.bib23)\]. ServeLearnBench separates serving and
held-out test tasks within each window and includes learning calls in
its resource accounting \[[24](#bib.bib24)\].

### 2.2 Task Streams and Metrics

We record a task’s outcome before using its feedback to update the
agent. Let $`x_{1},\ldots,x_{T}`$ be the ordered tasks, $`\theta`$ the
fixed model parameters, and $`s_{t}`$ the state used for task $`t`$.
Execution produces a trajectory and a binary verification outcome:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\tau_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x_{t},s_{t}),\qquad y_{t}=V(x_{t},\tau_{t})\in\{0,1\}.
``` |  | (1) |

Updates use completed-task history
$`\mathcal{H}_{t}=\{(x_{i},\tau_{i},y_{i}):i\leq t\}`$, restricted by
the state boundaries and support windows. They may read public
instructions, visible trajectories, and scalar outcomes, but not future
tasks, reference solutions, or hidden test contents. Tokens spent
re-executing completed tasks are charged to the RSI Tax; these runs do
not replace the tasks’ original outcomes.

Repository tasks come from seven selected 15-task chains in
SWE-Chain-Evo, totaling 105 positions \[[25](#bib.bib25)\]. Learned
state persists within each chain and resets between chains; each task
starts from its prescribed repository snapshot. Terminal-Bench 2.1
supplies 89 heterogeneous tasks in a fixed order, with learned state
retained throughout \[[26](#bib.bib26)\]. Ordering these independent
tasks allows cross-task reuse but does not introduce environmental
drift.

For a prefix of length $`t`$, we define

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
Q(t)=\sum_{i=1}^{t}y_{i},\qquad A(t)=\frac{Q(t)}{t},\qquad N(t)=N_{\rm task}(t)+N_{\rm RSI}(t).
``` |  | (2) |

$`N(t)`$ includes the tokens used for task execution and the RSI Tax
incurred through that position. We report final accuracy $`A(T)`$ and
total tokens $`N(T)`$;
Section [3](#S3 "3 The RSI Tax ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost")
specifies the token accounting. Sequential reuse of experience overlaps
with continual learning. Our objective is the accuracy and cost of
serving the arriving tasks, while concurrent work on self-evolving
agents evaluates retention across task families \[[27](#bib.bib27)\].

### 2.3 Experimental Settings

We compare Static, ReasoningBank, EvoSkill, Meta-Harness, RRSI, and SRN
(Section [4](#S4 "4 Simple Reflection with Notes (SRN) ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost"))
using DeepSeek V4.1 Flash \[[28](#bib.bib28)\] and GPT-6
Luna \[[29](#bib.bib29)\]. This gives
$`6\times 2\times(105+89)=2{,}328`$ scored method–task pairs. Within
each model–benchmark setting, the methods share the task order, initial
KIRA agent, and nominal execution limits.

SRN, Meta-Harness, and EvoSkill update every four completed tasks and
hold the selected state fixed within each window. Parallel tasks in a
window do not receive one another’s feedback. Their support sets contain
the two most recent tasks on DeepSeek/SWE and four tasks in the other
settings. ReasoningBank retains per-task retrieval and memory updates,
without its separate memory-aware test-time scaling component.

The original EvoSkill procedure is adapted to changing support sets by
re-scoring its existing frontier. Our Meta-Harness selector requires a
strict accuracy improvement to change the deployment. We also retain the
methods’ feedback choices: SRN selects failures using official scalar
outcomes, while ReasoningBank uses its internal trajectory judge. Model
parameters and implementation details are in
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Experimental Protocol ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost").

## 3 The RSI Tax

### 3.1 Cost Accounting

For a recorded model call $`c`$, let $`n(c)`$ be its input-plus-output
usage. Task-execution calls $`\mathcal{C}_{\rm task}`$ and
self-improvement calls $`\mathcal{C}_{\rm RSI}`$ are disjoint. The
absolute RSI Tax and its rate are

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle N_{\rm task}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{\rm task}}n(c),`$ | $`\displaystyle N_{\rm RSI}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{\rm RSI}}n(c),`$ |  | (3) |
|  | $`\displaystyle\rho_{\rm RSI}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\frac{N_{\rm RSI}}{N_{\rm task}},`$ | $`\displaystyle N_{\rm total}`$ | $`\displaystyle=N_{\rm task}+N_{\rm RSI}.`$ |  |  |

The tax includes the tokens spent producing or evaluating an update,
regardless of whether that update is adopted. Reading learned state
during task execution belongs to $`N_{\rm task}`$. Embedding tokens are
included in the RSI Tax under Explore. The RSI Tax accounts for
$`\rho_{\rm RSI}/(1+\rho_{\rm RSI})`$ of total token usage; at a Tax
rate of 100%, it equals task-execution cost. We compare token costs
within each model setting.

Relative to a reference method $`b`$, the net token premium is

|     |                                                     |     |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \Delta N_{m,b}=N_{{\rm total},m}-N_{{\rm total},b}.
       ```                                                  |     | (4) |

We compare this premium with task accuracy. We next break down the RSI
Tax by operation and by subsequent use of the associated state or
artifact.

### 3.2 Decomposing RSI Tax

We report verification, exploration, and writing separately, while
retaining the reported *Other* residual
(Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Write. ‣ 3.2 Decomposing RSI Tax ‣ 3 The RSI Tax ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost")).

##### Verify.

Verification evaluates an incumbent or candidate on completed support
tasks to inform selection. It includes baseline validation, candidate
smoke tests and further validation, and re-evaluation of an existing
skill frontier. Verification performed during the original task
execution remains in $`N_{\rm task}`$.

##### Explore.

Exploration gathers or analyzes experience used to propose an update. It
includes extra task rollouts, proposal generation without artifact
edits, trajectory judgment, and ReasoningBank’s embedding calls.

##### Write.

Writing creates or revises persistent state, including harness code,
skills, notes, and memories. For Meta-Harness, trajectory analysis and
candidate search are charged to Explore, and candidate-code edits to
Write. EvoSkill likewise separates skill proposals from materialization.
SRN combines note analysis and revision in one operation, which is
charged entirely to Write. Each cost item is counted once.

| Method |  Verify |  Explore |  Write |
|----|----|----|----|
| ReasoningBank |  — |  Trajectory judgment; embeddings |  Memory extraction |
| Meta-Harness |  Incumbent and candidate validation |  Trajectory analysis; candidate search |  Candidate harness editing |
| EvoSkill |  Initial, new-skill, and frontier validation |  Extra rollouts; skill proposals |  Skill materialization |
| RRSI |  Incumbent and candidate validation |  Trajectory analysis and summarization |  Candidate harness generation and revision |
| SRN |  — |  — |  Joint note analysis and revision |

Table 1: RSI operations in the three cost categories. Token totals also
retain a separate Other residual, reported in
Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Aggregate Costs and Subsequent Use ‣ Appendix C Detailed Token Results ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost").

### 3.3 Use in Subsequent Tasks

We classify costs within the RSI Tax by whether the associated state or
artifact is used in a subsequent task before the next reset or the end
of the stream. Use includes running an updated harness, using a skill
during execution, or adding a revised note or retrieved memory to the
agent’s task context. Verification and exploration costs follow their
recorded association with a state or artifact; attribution is not
limited to the final writing call. The labels record subsequent use, not
a measured effect on task behavior or accuracy.

Let $`p(c)\in\{V,E,W,O\}`$ identify the cost category of RSI call $`c`$
(verification, exploration, writing, or Other), and $`d(c)\in\{1,0\}`$
the use status of its associated state or artifact. Then

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
N_{p,d}=\sum_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{\rm RSI}}n(c)\,\mathbf{1}\{p(c)=p,\ d(c)=d\},\qquad N_{\rm total}=N_{\rm task}+\sum_{p\in\{V,E,W,O\}}\sum_{d\in\{0,1\}}N_{p,d}.
``` |  | (5) |

The share of the RSI Tax associated with unused state or artifacts is

|     |                                                            |     |     |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       r_{\rm no\text{-}use}=\frac{\sum_{p}N_{p,0}}{N_{\rm RSI}}.
       ```                                                         |     | (6) |

This is a share of tokens, not a fraction of updates or artifacts.
Section [5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Cost Breakdown and Subsequent Use ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost")
reports costs by category and use status $`N_{p,d}`$, with category
totals $`N_{p}=\sum_{d}N_{p,d}`$ and use-status totals
$`N_{d}=\sum_{p}N_{p,d}`$.
Appendix [B.3](#A2.SS3 "B.3 Cost Categories and Subsequent Use ‣ Appendix B Accounting and Interpretation ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost")
describes aggregation and precision, and
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Illustrative Update Traces ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost")
provides supplementary event diagnostics.

## 4 Simple Reflection with Notes (SRN)

SRN is a bounded-note baseline based on cumulative-note
adaptation \[[9](#bib.bib9)\]. At each four-task update, SRN uses scalar
verifier outcomes to select failed tasks for note revision; it includes
the current note in later task contexts. The note is limited to 2,048
tokens.

At an update boundary, let $`m`$ be the current note and
$`\mathcal{W}_{t}`$ the permitted recent window. The update is

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{F}_{t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\{(x_{i},\tau_{i},y_{i})\in\mathcal{W}_{t}:y_{i}=0\},`$ |  | (7) |
|  | $`\displaystyle m^{+}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\begin{cases}m,&\mathcal{F}_{t}=\varnothing,\\
\operatorname{Limit}_{2048}\!\left(G_{\theta}(m,\operatorname{Excerpt}(\mathcal{F}_{t}))\right),&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}`$ |  |  |

The generator receives the previous note, public instructions, fixed
trajectory excerpts, and scalar outcomes. A valid nonempty revision is
adopted directly; an invalid response leaves the note unchanged.
Appendix [A.4](#A1.SS4 "A.4 Note Baseline and Prompt ‣ Appendix A Experimental Protocol ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost")
gives the prompt and excerpt limits.

SRN performs no extra task sampling, candidate validation, or retrieval
search. Its total cost includes note construction and the complete
execution cost of solving tasks with the note. It provides a low-cost
adaptive comparison, although the experiment does not isolate the effect
of each design choice.

## 5 Experiments

We compare accuracy and total token cost, then break down the RSI Tax by
operation and subsequent use. Accounting details are given in
Appendix [B.1](#A2.SS1 "B.1 Token and Outcome Accounting ‣ Appendix B Accounting and Interpretation ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost").

### 5.1 Accuracy and End-to-End Cost

Table [2](#S5.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 5.1 Accuracy and End-to-End Cost ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost")

Figure [2](#S5.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 5.1 Accuracy and End-to-End Cost ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost")
compare the six methods. SRN has the highest observed accuracy in three
settings and ties EvoSkill in the fourth, while using fewer total tokens
than Meta-Harness, EvoSkill, and RRSI in every setting. ReasoningBank
incurs a smaller RSI Tax than these three methods but does not
consistently improve accuracy over Static.

Table 2: Accuracy and total token cost. Accuracy is in percent; Total is
in millions of input-plus-output tokens and includes both task-execution
cost and the RSI Tax. DeepSeek denotes DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. Bold marks
the highest accuracy and lowest total cost in each setting, including
ties. Detailed subtotals and accounting conventions are in
Appendices [C.1](#A3.SS1 "C.1 Task Tokens and RSI Tax ‣ Appendix C Detailed Token Results ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost")

Relative to Static, SRN gains 4.7 percentage points in mean accuracy
with a 3.6% mean increase in total tokens. The mean token reductions
relative to Meta-Harness, EvoSkill, and RRSI are 65.6%, 71.0%, and
68.2%, respectively. These summaries weight the four settings equally:
accuracy gains are averaged differences, while token changes are
computed as within-setting ratios before averaging. SRN’s update calls
account for less than 0.4% of its total tokens; task execution,
including use of the note, accounts for the rest.

The relation between accuracy and total token cost varies across
settings. On the DeepSeek terminal stream, Static uses the fewest tokens
(185.55M), while SRN uses 15.7% more and gains 9.0 percentage points in
observed accuracy. On the GPT-6 Luna repository stream, SRN uses 156.67M
task-execution tokens compared with Static’s 179.69M, a difference that
more than offsets its 0.40M update cost. Its total is 12.6% lower than
Static’s and its accuracy is 2.9 points higher.

##### Execution cost and total cost.

Omitting the RSI Tax can reverse the cost comparison. On the DeepSeek
terminal stream, Meta-Harness uses fewer task-execution tokens than SRN
(184.13M versus 214.37M). Its 578.45M RSI Tax, however, raises the total
to 762.57M, compared with SRN’s 214.65M, while its observed accuracy is
slightly lower (77.5% versus 78.7%). These task totals cover all
deployed states used during the stream, rather than a separate
evaluation of the final checkpoint.

##### Sources of the RSI Tax.

Verification accounts for 74.8% of Meta-Harness’s RSI Tax, 78.1% of
EvoSkill’s, and 93.6% of RRSI’s after aggregation over the four
settings. EvoSkill also spends 455.29M tokens on additional rollouts and
proposals, compared with 4.59M on skill materialization. ReasoningBank
divides its cost almost equally between exploration (judgment and
embeddings) and memory writing. SRN spends 1.21M tokens on its joint
note-analysis and revision operation. Full component totals are given in
Appendix [C.2](#A3.SS2 "C.2 Aggregate Costs and Subsequent Use ‣ Appendix C Detailed Token Results ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost").

Verification repeatedly runs the agent on support tasks, often
evaluating several candidate or retained programs per update. On the
DeepSeek terminal stream, EvoSkill spends 497.45M tokens refreshing its
old frontier, compared with 182.26M on the 89 arriving tasks.
Re-evaluating existing programs alone therefore costs more than serving
the task stream, before accounting for extra rollouts or new-skill
validation. Recorded input accounts for approximately 98.1% of the RSI
Tax in both Meta-Harness and EvoSkill.

##### Costs associated with subsequent use.

Under the attribution in
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Use in Subsequent Tasks ‣ 3 The RSI Tax ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost"),
52.78% of Meta-Harness’s RSI Tax, 37.91% of EvoSkill’s, 63.57% of
ReasoningBank’s, and 23.70% of RRSI’s are associated with states or
artifacts that are not used in later tasks. All reported SRN update cost
is associated with notes supplied to subsequent executions. These
percentages describe token expenditure, not the frequency of successful
updates or an effect on accuracy.
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Detailed Token Results ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost")
gives the component totals and
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Illustrative Update Traces ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost")
examines individual update traces.

The same lack of subsequent use can involve different operations.
Meta-Harness assigns 564.85M verification tokens, 217.60M exploration
tokens, and 69.22M writing tokens to candidates not used later. For
ReasoningBank, the corresponding costs are 15.51M for judgment and
embeddings and 15.63M for memory extraction. The breakdown identifies
different sources of RSI Tax in these two methods; their overall shares
of costs without subsequent use do not reveal this composition.

## 6 Discussion

The results show that the RSI Tax can exceed the cost of executing the
task stream. We discuss how this changes the design of update policies,
where costs might be reduced, and what the current evidence can
establish.

##### Choosing an update policy.

An RSI update policy should pursue continued gains in agent capabilities
as tasks arrive while controlling the RSI Tax. Its efficiency objective
should include the immediate update cost, expected task-execution cost,
and the cost of subsequent RSI updates over the remaining tasks. Such a
policy could retain the current state, update memory or skills, or
generate and evaluate harness changes. Repeated reuse may justify a
larger initial investment \[[18](#bib.bib18)\]. Our experiments compare
fixed procedures and realized costs; they do not evaluate a policy that
forecasts these costs and selects updates.

##### Reducing the RSI Tax.

When verification dominates the RSI Tax, reducing the cost of candidate
evaluation becomes a priority. Support-task selection and frontier
maintenance are therefore natural targets for reducing update cost.
Adaptive validation-task selection already provides one
approach \[[17](#bib.bib17)\]. The subsequent-use analysis also
motivates more selective construction of skills and memories. Whether
these changes reduce total tokens while preserving task performance
requires controlled evaluation. Reducing update cost complements the
execution-cost objectives used in cost-aware harness
selection \[[12](#bib.bib12), [13](#bib.bib13)\].

##### Limitations.

The evaluation covers two backbone models, seven repository chains, and
one ordering of a terminal benchmark. Other models, workloads,
orderings, and repeated runs are needed to assess the stability of the
observed comparisons. The cost attribution is descriptive: use in a
later task does not establish an accuracy benefit, and the absence of
such use does not establish that the associated calls can be removed
without changing later updates or task outcomes. Controlled
interventions are needed to measure the effects of reducing each cost
component.

## 7 Conclusion

We evaluate the end-to-end token cost and task performance of mainstream
RSI methods on task streams, using SRN as a simple adaptive baseline. We
introduce the RSI Tax to quantify the token cost of the self-improvement
process during deployment. On the studied streams, SRN shows that
competitive task accuracy need not require a large RSI Tax. Decomposing
the RSI Tax into verification, exploration, and writing costs shows that
repeated verification can consume more tokens than executing the task
stream itself. A substantial share of the RSI Tax is also associated
with states or artifacts that are not used in subsequent tasks. These
findings motivate RSI agents that jointly optimize the RSI Tax incurred
by trial-and-error self-improvement and expected task-execution cost
while ensuring continued growth in agent capabilities across the task
stream.

## Appendix A Experimental Protocol

### A.1 Streams, State Boundaries, and Model Parameters

The reported SWE-Chain-Evo subset uses Click, CoreDNS, NATS, Fiber,
Loki, Istio, and Prometheus, each with 15 ordered task positions. These
105 positions are a selected subset of EvoArena, whose full
SWE-Chain-Evo benchmark contains 50 chains and 493 chain-step
instances \[[25](#bib.bib25)\]. Notes, memories, skills, and harness
state reset at chain boundaries. Each task starts from its
benchmark-prescribed repository snapshot; earlier agent patches are not
transplanted into later tasks. The current repository and public history
remain available to all methods, including Static. The terminal
evaluation uses all 89 Terminal-Bench 2.1 tasks in one fixed order with
task-specific environments and persistent learned state across the
stream.

The recorded router identifiers are deepseek/deepseek-v4.1-flash and
openai/gpt-6-luna. Official model documentation is provided by [DeepSeek
\[28\]](#bib.bib28), [OpenAI \[29\]](#bib.bib29). The recorded harness
configuration specifies high reasoning effort for both models, a nominal
262,144-token context limit, a nominal 65,536-token per-call output
limit, and at most 100 agent turns, without a cumulative per-task token
cap. These are harness-imposed limits, not the maximum capacities
advertised by the providers. DeepSeek uses temperature 1 and top-$`p`$
0.95; the reported GPT-6 Luna configuration omits both sampling
parameters. Model-specific tokenization means that nominal limits do not
imply identical effective capacity. SWE solving and verification limits
are 7,200 and 600 seconds; terminal tasks use their official
task-specific limits.

### A.2 Periodic Updates and Support Sets

SRN, Meta-Harness, and EvoSkill have an update opportunity after every
four completed tasks, with no final partial-window update. There are
three opportunities per repository chain and 22 per terminal stream.
Periodic methods freeze the selected state within each four-task window;
parallel execution does not expose another task’s feedback inside that
window. ReasoningBank retains its per-task memory workflow.

The DeepSeek V4.1 Flash repository experiments use the most recent two
tasks as update support; the other three settings use the most recent
four. Thus, the four-task *update interval* is shared, while support
size differs between those settings. Comparisons are made within each
setting before macro averaging; support size is held fixed within a
setting. Re-evaluating support tasks supplies scalar feedback for future
updates, not replacements for their earlier formal outcomes.

### A.3 Method Configurations

Static retains the initial KIRA execution policy and no learned
cross-task state. The reported Meta-Harness configuration permits one
native search iteration per update, with smoke evaluation and
support-set validation. Its deployment adapter requires a strict
improvement in mean validation accuracy and retains the incumbent on a
tie. Subsequent tasks run under the selected harness. This rule is
narrower than the population-based search described by the original
method \[[11](#bib.bib11)\]; the saturated-selector case concerns this
evaluated deployment rule.

RRSI’s update procedure includes an analyst and trajectory digesters, a
proposer, a critic, and validation. The analyst and digesters examine
past trajectories and summarize failure modes and reusable behavior; the
proposer constructs candidate harness edits. The critic separately
screens candidate changes before validation \[[12](#bib.bib12)\].

The reported EvoSkill configuration uses the upstream proposal, skill
materialization, and program-selection operators with one native
iteration, a frontier size of three, and one sampling category
containing two samples. Existing frontier members are re-scored on the
current support set as the window moves. The original algorithm uses a
fixed validation set and evaluates new candidates \[[10](#bib.bib10)\].
The rolling refresh is part of our streaming implementation and its full
recorded cost is charged. The original proposer may inspect ground-truth
answers; our information boundary permits only public instructions,
visible traces, and scalar feedback from completed tasks. The selected
skill catalog is made available to the agent through the existing
skill-discovery interface. These runs use the original EvoSkill
procedure; EvoSkill v2 instead adopts each epoch’s skill revision
without validation-based rejection \[[30](#bib.bib30)\].

ReasoningBank preserves trajectory judgment, memory extraction, and
retrieval of the highest-ranked episode bundle. A bundle can contain
multiple memory items; retrieving it adds those items to the agent’s
task context. ReasoningBank’s trajectory judge is distinct from the task
verifier used to calculate accuracy. Embedding uses
gemini-embedding-001; embedding tokens are included in the RSI Tax. This
evaluates the memory workflow without adding a separate
inference-scaling treatment.

### A.4 Note Baseline and Prompt

SRN maintains a note of at most 2,048 tokens and uses the same backbone
for note updates and task execution. The generator receives the previous
note, public instructions, scalar outcomes, and excerpts from failed
trajectories. Each excerpt contains the first 20,000 and last 10,000
characters, or the full trajectory when shorter. A valid, nonempty
response replaces the note; an invalid response leaves it unchanged.
Oversized notes are truncated by the configured tokenizer. Each update
uses one logical generation, and all retry calls remain in the token
count.

The terminal note prompt is reproduced below; the repository prompt uses
the same constraints in the repository-chain setting.

> Maintain a short experience note for a terminal agent learning acrossa
> chronological sequence of independent tasks. Use only the
> suppliedprevious note, public task instructions, visible execution
> traces, andscalar verifier rewards.Return only the replacement note in
> plain Markdown. Keep the finalnote within 2048 tokens. Keep useful
> earlier lessons, remove outdatedor unsupported claims, and add
> reusable lessons supported by thecurrent evidence. Prefer concrete
> environment inspection, tool-use,debugging, implementation, and
> verification advice. Distinguishobserved facts from hypotheses. Do not
> infer hidden tests or referencesolutions, invent command results, or
> include instructions to accessfuture tasks. Do not solve the next
> task, request tools, or repeat afull task-specific patch. Experience
> is guidance; future tasks maychange the relevant assumptions.Trace
> excerpts use a fixed head/tail view and may omit intermediatesteps. A
> scalar reward of zero does not establish a specific rootcause. Avoid
> drawing strong causal lessons without supporting visibleevidence. An
> empty useful update may retain the previous note. Outputa note,
> without surrounding explanation.

## Appendix B Accounting and Interpretation

### B.1 Token and Outcome Accounting

The task-execution total includes context management and reading
retained state. The RSI Tax includes tokens spent on memory
construction, embeddings, proposal sessions, extra sampling, and
candidate and incumbent validation. Request identities prevent
double-counting across logs. Input and output tokens are included;
cached input remains in the count, and reasoning tokens already included
in provider output are not added a second time. The per-setting stage
sums reconcile with the corresponding RSI totals in
Table [4](#A3.T4 "Table 4 ‣ C.1 Task Tokens and RSI Tax ‣ Appendix C Detailed Token Results ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost"),
subject to display rounding. These totals measure token use rather than
monetary cost, which also depends on the pricing of input, output, and
cached tokens \[[31](#bib.bib31)\].

Accuracy summarizes task outcomes under the streaming protocol in
Section [2.2](#S2.SS2 "2.2 Task Streams and Metrics ‣ 2 Evaluation Setup ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost").
Tokens spent on support-set validation are charged to the RSI Tax;
validation scores do not replace the earlier task outcomes.

### B.2 Cross-Setting Summaries

Let $`A_{m,g}`$ denote fractional accuracy and $`N_{m,g}`$ total tokens
for method $`m`$ in setting $`g`$. For comparison method $`b`$, we
report

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta A_{b}=\frac{100}{4}\sum_{g=1}^{4}(A_{\mathrm{SRN{}},g}-A_{b,g}),\qquad S_{b}=\frac{100}{4}\sum_{g=1}^{4}\left(1-\frac{N_{\mathrm{SRN{}},g}}{N_{b,g}}\right).
``` |  | (8) |

The unrounded records give $`\Delta A_{\rm Static}=4.714`$ percentage
points, $`S_{\rm Static}=-3.616\%`$,
$`S_{\rm Meta\text{-}Harness}=65.588\%`$, $`S_{\rm EvoSkill}=70.994\%`$,
and $`S_{\rm RRSI}=68.242\%`$. The mean accuracy difference relative to
RRSI is 4.238 percentage points. Each model–benchmark setting receives
equal weight. Token ratios are formed within settings before averaging.

### B.3 Cost Categories and Subsequent Use

We report verification, exploration, and writing costs alongside the
Other residual from the source records, and separately track whether the
associated state or artifact is used in later tasks.
Figure [3](#S5.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 5.2 Cost Breakdown and Subsequent Use ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost")(b)
reports the resulting breakdown, with every segment normalized by the
method’s complete RSI Tax.

The accounting is a sum over the four model–environment settings, in
millions of input-plus-output tokens. Summing the available per-setting
stage totals reproduces the corresponding aggregate RSI Tax, up to
display rounding. This aggregate measures token volume, not a common
physical-compute unit across different model tokenizers. Comparative
ratios in the main results are computed within settings before
averaging.

Cells, totals, and percentages are independently rounded, generally to
two decimal places; RRSI’s Other cost is reported as 0.009M (less than
0.01% of the RSI Tax). Independently rounded cells need not sum exactly
to the displayed totals. In particular, Meta-Harness’s use-status rows
sum to 297.00M Explore and 91.73M Write, while the separately reported
category totals are 296.99M and 91.74M. RRSI’s 0.009M Other cost belongs
to the row without subsequent use. RRSI’s aggregate RSI Tax is 1,770.50M
tokens: 1,350.81M with subsequent use and 419.69M without subsequent
use. For methods with separately reported full-precision total and RSI
counts, task tokens are computed as their difference. RRSI’s aggregate
task-execution cost is approximately 956.56M tokens, computed as
2,727.06M total tokens minus the rounded 1,770.50M RSI total and subject
to that rounding precision.

The operation-to-category mapping is given in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ Write. ‣ 3.2 Decomposing RSI Tax ‣ 3 The RSI Tax ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost").
Meta-Harness’s proposal sessions total 414.969432M tokens, comprising
296.99M Explore, 91.74M Write, and 26.24M Other; these amounts sum to
414.97M at the reported precision. The per-setting stage tables below
report proposal sessions as a combined category, while
Table [5](#A3.T5 "Table 5 ‣ C.2 Aggregate Costs and Subsequent Use ‣ Appendix C Detailed Token Results ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost")
gives their aggregate cost breakdown. SRN’s joint note-analysis and
revision calls belong to Write.

### B.4 Linking Costs to Subsequent Execution

We attribute each cost item to the state or artifact it concerns,
including items incurred during verification or exploration. For a
harness, subsequent use means execution under the associated controller;
for skills, notes, and memories, it means their use during task
execution or inclusion in the agent’s context. Each cost item
contributes once to the table; shared verification or analysis costs
follow the designated candidate. Attribution follows the recorded
association and subsequent use before reset or the end of the stream. A
round-level comparison of the deployed state alone does not give the
same classification, because a round may inspect multiple artifacts. Use
is recorded separately from changes in accuracy.

##### Input and output.

Across all settings, recorded input accounts for approximately 98.1% of
the RSI Tax for both Meta-Harness and EvoSkill. These totals are
consistent with repeated processing of growing execution contexts, but
input dominance alone does not identify redundancy. Exact input/output
attribution requires per-call usage; matching character sequences can
establish repeated inclusion of trajectory text, but cannot determine
token allocation within a prompt.

## Appendix D Illustrative Update Traces

The following diagnostics examine proposal generation, acceptance
decisions, and memory retrieval in individual update traces. They use
different observation units and do not form an additive partition of the
RSI Tax. Observing one of these events does not establish that removing
its calls would preserve later performance.

### D.1 Event Criteria

Table [9](#A4.T9 "Table 9 ‣ D.1 Event Criteria ‣ Appendix D Illustrative Update Traces ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost")
summarizes the criteria.

|  Pattern |  Failure criterion |  Unit and observation point |
|----|----|----|
|  Proposal-free search |  A search round consumes tokens but emits no proposal. |  Search round; after it ends. |
|  Decision-invariant evaluation |  All possible validation results lead to the same acceptance decision. |  Candidate-evaluation calls; condition known before evaluation. |
|  Unretrieved memory |  A stored bundle has later task opportunities but is never retrieved before reset. |  Bundle construction; retrieval observed through the remaining stream. |

Table 9: Supplementary event criteria for individual update traces.
These diagnostics concern proposal generation, acceptance decisions, and
retrieval.

#### D.1.1 Proposal-Free Search

For a method that runs candidate search, let $`C_{u}`$ be the recorded
cost of round $`u`$, and let $`q_{u}`$ count new proposals emitted by
its proposer. A round is proposal-free when $`C_{u}>0`$ and $`q_{u}=0`$.
A proposal is counted before materialization or validation, including
one that later fails to build. Re-scoring an existing candidate does not
create a new proposal.

This pattern concerns failure to produce a proposed update, not the
absence of every possible benefit from search. A method may still select
a previously evaluated candidate when $`q_{u}=0`$, so deployment changes
must be recorded separately.

#### D.1.2 Decision-Invariant Evaluation

Fix the proposal, the acceptance rule, and all information available
before candidate evaluation. Let $`A_{u,c}(v)\in\{0,1\}`$ be the
decision to accept candidate $`c`$ at update $`u`$ if validation returns
$`v`$. Let $`\mathcal{V}_{u,c}`$ contain the validation outcomes not
ruled out by that pre-evaluation information. Evaluation is
decision-invariant when

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
A_{u,c}(v)=A_{u,c}(v^{\prime})\quad\text{for all }v,v^{\prime}\in\mathcal{V}_{u,c}.
``` |  | (9) |

Thus, no possible result can change acceptance; an observed rejection
alone does not establish this condition. The recorded example is the
always-reject case: the incumbent scores 1, accuracy is bounded by 1,
and only a strict improvement on the same support set is accepted. A
rule that also rewards lower execution cost could still accept a
candidate at equal accuracy; it would require a different analysis.

The charged unit is candidate evaluation after this condition becomes
known. Incumbent evaluation used to establish the score, and analysis or
proposal generation in the same round, are not automatically part of the
diagnostic.
Section [D.2.2](#A4.SS2.SSS2 "D.2.2 Decision-Invariant Evaluation ‣ D.2 Case Studies ‣ Appendix D Illustrative Update Traces ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost")
applies this test to the strict selector used in our Meta-Harness
implementation.

#### D.1.3 Unretrieved Memory

For a retrieval-based memory bank, let $`b_{a}`$ be the judgment and
extraction cost of stored bundle $`a`$, $`h_{a}`$ its remaining eligible
task opportunities, and $`r_{a}`$ its retrieval count before the next
reset. Construction is classified as unretrieved when $`h_{a}>0`$ and
$`r_{a}=0`$, with total cost

|     |                                                      |     |      |
|-----|------------------------------------------------------|-----|------|
|     |
       ``` math
       N_{\rm unretrieved}=\sum_{a:h_{a}>0,\,r_{a}=0}b_{a}.
       ```                                                   |     | (10) |

The unit is a bundle, which may contain several memory items. We exclude
updates that produce no bundle and construction after the final task.
Embedding tokens remain in total RSI usage but are not assigned to
bundle construction.

Retrieval records whether a bundle’s contents entered the agent’s task
context, not whether they were useful. A bundle can remain unretrieved
because later tasks do not need it; remaining task opportunities do not
establish semantic relevance. The criterion identifies a construction
cost that receives no retrieval during the observed horizon, rather than
proving the memory incorrect or permanently useless.

### D.2 Case Studies

We now apply the three criteria in their defined order
(Figure [4](#A4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ D.2 Case Studies ‣ Appendix D Illustrative Update Traces ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost")).
Proposal-free search and decision-invariant evaluation are illustrated
by individual traces; the unretrieved-memory diagnostic also has
aggregate construction costs satisfying its predicate. Their prevalence
should not be inferred from the stage totals above.

Figure 4: Illustrative update traces. Left: a search round without a
proposal. Middle: candidate evaluation whose result cannot change
acceptance. Right: a stored memory bundle with no later retrieval. The
first two examples depend on the online implementation choices described
in
Section [2.3](#S2.SS3 "2.3 Experimental Settings ‣ 2 Evaluation Setup ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost").

#### D.2.1 Proposal-Free Search

After task 68 in the DeepSeek EvoSkill run, three existing programs are
evaluated on four support tasks at a cost of 44,882,109 tokens. The
method then spends 13,282,793 tokens on two additional trajectories.
Both succeed, leaving no failed sample to trigger the proposer. The
complete round costs 58,164,902 tokens, produces no new proposal, and
retains iter-skill-7.

Most tokens in this round are spent re-evaluating the existing frontier
before a new proposal is available. The repeated refresh comes from the
rolling support window in our implementation; EvoSkill’s original
algorithm uses a fixed validation set. The case motivates testing
whether such maintenance can be deferred or reduced when the proposal
step has no new change to offer.

#### D.2.2 Decision-Invariant Evaluation

After task 72 in the GPT-6 Luna Meta-Harness run, the incumbent scores
100% on the support set and the selector requires a strictly higher
accuracy. Its acceptance function is therefore zero for every possible
candidate score. Nevertheless, the new candidate receives a 69,715-token
smoke test and 534,126 tokens of further validation.

The diagnostic covers the 603,841 candidate-evaluation tokens, rather
than all 4,002,438 tokens in the update. Incumbent evaluation may be
needed to establish the saturation condition. This example concerns our
strict deployment rule; the original Meta-Harness population search does
not require it. The identified calls cannot change the immediate
acceptance decision, although their traces may inform later search.

#### D.2.3 Unretrieved Memory

For task 55, caffe-cifar-10, in the DeepSeek ReasoningBank run, judgment
and extraction cost 117,631 and 124,108 tokens. They produce one bundle
of three items concerning the build and verification task. None of the
34 remaining tasks retrieves that bundle. The bundle therefore
contributes 241,739 construction tokens to $`N_{\rm unretrieved}`$ in
Equation [10](#A4.E10 "In D.1.3 Unretrieved Memory ‣ D.1 Event Criteria ‣ Appendix D Illustrative Update Traces ‣ The RSI Tax:When Recursive Self-Improvement Is Not Worth the Cost").

This narrower unretrieved-bundle diagnostic excludes several costs that
the main accounting can classify as having no subsequent use. Applying
its predicate to all available memory records gives 53.1%–61.5% of
ReasoningBank RSI tokens. On terminal tasks, the corresponding
construction costs are 5.16M of 8.61M RSI tokens for DeepSeek and 3.62M
of 5.88M for GPT-6 Luna. The numerator excludes embeddings, updates
without a stored bundle, and construction without a later task
opportunity; the denominator includes all RSI tokens. These are cost
shares, not fractions of memory items.
````
